clue.text: The person in charge is a knob

definitions.meaning: the everyday sense: the one telling everybody else what to do
the craftsman's sense: a round projecting stud on a shield, a door or a church ceiling

explanation.surface: Someone writing off the person who runs the place as an idiot.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Knob' is an insult on the surface and a piece of ironmongery in the second definition — the round projection at the centre of a shield or a vault.
explanation.definitionFit: The boss is whoever gives the orders, and a boss is also the raised stud at the centre of a shield or a vaulted ceiling.

clue.text: Cause excessive strain to old, old monarch: that's clear all round

indicators.note: Something that goes all round a thing encloses it on every side, so the word beside it splits open and the other pieces sit in the gap.

parts.note: overt means out in the open rather than concealed — 'clear' in the sense of plain to see
an ex is an old partner, and ex- fronts any former job title
ER is Elizabeth Regina, the late Queen, and the crossword's standard monarch

explanation.surface: Telling an ancient ruler not to wear himself out, in front of everybody.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Old, old' is two separate instructions rather than repetition for emphasis: the first is the ex- of an ex-husband, the second belongs to the monarch.
explanation.definitionFit: To overexert yourself is to push yourself too hard: the 'over-' carries 'excessive' and the 'exert' carries 'strain'.

clue.text: Small business held up by No 10? It's a sign

indicators.note: Whatever holds something up is underneath it, so the piece named next goes below the ones already assembled — which in a down entry means last.

parts.note: s = small, the label on the smallest shirt in the shop
corp is short for corporation, a business
the figures 1 and 0 read as letters: the Roman one, then the round nought

explanation.surface: The government propping up a struggling small firm.
explanation.walkthrough: No 10 is the prime minister's house in Downing Street, which is why the sentence reads as politics; the wordplay wants nothing but the two characters the number is written with.
explanation.definitionFit: Scorpio is one of the twelve signs of the zodiac, so 'a sign' names it by the class it belongs to.

clue.text: A system? Not at home

parts.note: the first word is taken at face value, one letter as written
the manner in which something is done is its system or method

explanation.surface: Asking whether there is any method here, and finding nobody in.
explanation.walkthrough: The question mark does the hiding: it makes 'A system?' read as a doubtful aside rather than as two pieces laid end to end.
explanation.definitionFit: Away means not in — the word on the answerphone, and the word on a fixture list for a match played at the other team's ground.

clue.text: Australian, a little tease, to prove alluring — or try

indicators.note: A little of a word is only its start, so a single opening letter is wanted rather than the word itself.

parts.note: a = Australian, the standard abbreviation
the first letter of the word is all that is taken
to tempt somebody is to prove alluring to them

explanation.surface: An Australian flirt turning on the charm.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Australian' looks like the opening of a character sketch and is a single letter; 'a little tease' looks like more of the sketch and is another one.
explanation.definitionFit: An attempt at something is a try at it — the two nouns swap freely, as in 'give it a try'.

clue.text: Dined at home from single can, reportedly

indicators.note: Something reported is heard rather than read, so the words are wanted as a noise — and the spelling that noise gets written with is a different one.

parts.note: a single one of anything is simply 'a'
a can is a tin, and it is those two pieces run together — 'a tin' — that get said out loud

explanation.surface: Somebody insisting they had supper at home out of one solitary tin.
explanation.walkthrough: Say 'a tin' at speed and the join between the two words shifts, which is the whole of the mechanism; 'single' is doing nothing more than handing over a bare article.
explanation.definitionFit: To eat in is to have your meal at home instead of going out for it, and the past tense matches 'dined' exactly.

clue.text: Pretty vacant, taken in by hoax surveillance kit

indicators.note: A vacant building has nothing inside it, so the word in front keeps only its outermost letters and loses everything between them.

parts.note: a scam is a con or a hoax

indicators.note: To be taken in is to be admitted inside, so the letters just found go within the word named next.

parts.note: the first and last letters survive; the three in the middle are emptied out

explanation.surface: A good-looking airhead falling for a con.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Pretty Vacant' is a Sex Pistols single, which is why the two words read as one phrase rather than as an instruction, and 'taken in' means duped on the surface while it encloses in the wordplay.
explanation.definitionFit: A spycam is a camera small enough to be hidden in a room, which is the gear covert surveillance actually runs on.

clue.text: Islands separated? These hairlines might interlink, primarily!

definitions.text: Islands separated? These hairlines might interlink

indicators.note: Primarily means first of all, so it asks for the letter each of the words before it starts with.

parts.words: Islands separated? These hairlines might interlink
parts.note: six words, six opening letters, taken in the order they stand

explanation.surface: Islands that have drifted apart, with the thinnest of threads still tying them together.
explanation.walkthrough: The exclamation mark flags an all-in-one: the same six words define and also hand over the letters. A hairline is a line as thin as a hair, which is what a narrow land bridge looks like on a map.
explanation.definitionFit: An isthmus is a narrow neck of land joining two larger ones, so islands otherwise separated but tied by hairline strips is the plural read literally.

clue.text: In Athens, fat people edited film

indicators.note: An editor cuts the reel up and splices the pieces back in a new order, which is what happens to these letters.

parts.note: anagram fodder, fifteen letters

explanation.surface: Overweight Athenians cutting a movie together.
explanation.walkthrough: Fifteen letters with no obvious break makes the fodder hard to spot, and 'edited' sits exactly where a verb about film-making belongs, so it reads as part of the picture.
explanation.definitionFit: Planet of the Apes is the 1968 science-fiction picture, so 'film' points at it by example — the general word standing in for one title.

clue.text: Terrible mess, perhaps, setter's table

indicators.note: Perhaps marks the breed named next as only one instance, so the wordplay wants the general animal rather than that particular kind.

parts.note: a setter is a breed kept for pointing at game birds, and the possessive brings its article along with it
a house with a good table is one with good food — the meal served at it

explanation.surface: The crossword compiler's kitchen table, buried under a shocking mess.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Setter' is the compiler on the surface — Everyman talking about their own desk — and a breed of dog in the wordplay, which is the joke this setter gets to make every week.
explanation.definitionFit: A dog's dinner is British slang for something botched — you make a dog's dinner of a job — so the phrase means a terrible mess.

clue.text: Business bending paper-thin, vacuous regulations

indicators.note: Something bent has been forced out of its proper shape, and letters forced out of shape come back in a different order.

parts.note: anagram fodder, nine letters

indicators.note: A vacuous thing is empty inside, so the long word beside it keeps only the letters standing at its two ends.

parts.note: the outer pair only; the nine letters between them are emptied out

explanation.surface: A company quietly bending rules that were flimsy to start with.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Business' looks like the subject of a sentence about corner-cutting; it is the definition standing alone at the front, and every word after it is either fodder or instruction.
explanation.definitionFit: A partnership is a firm two or more people own and trade through, one of the standard legal shapes a business comes in.

clue.text: Detailed photo? Stop talking!

definitions.note: The first sense is a noun and the second an order barked at somebody, which is also why the answer takes a hyphen in one reading and not in the other.
definitions.meaning: the film-making sense: the camera brought right in on its subject
the barked sense: an order to keep quiet

explanation.surface: An impatient photographer telling a subject to be quiet.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Detailed' invites you to take the tail off some word, and that is the false path: it is doing nothing here but describing the photograph.
explanation.definitionFit: A close-up is the shot taken tight on a face, all detail; and 'close up!' is what you say to somebody you want to shut up.

clue.text: Pharaoh perhaps included in symposium on archaeology

indicators.note: Whatever is included in something sits inside it, so the letters are already there in the words that follow, in the order they are written.

parts.note: seven letters in a row, starting on the last letter of the first word and finishing inside the last

explanation.surface: A paper about Egypt given at an archaeology conference.
explanation.walkthrough: The join is the trick: the run starts at the very end of a long word, and 'on' — the sort of word the eye skips over — sits right in the middle of it.
explanation.definitionFit: A pharaoh was the sole ruler of ancient Egypt, so the word defines a monarch by example rather than by synonym.

clue.text: Inaccurately describe importers' bananas

indicators.note: Going bananas is going out of your mind, and letters out of their minds do not stay in the order they were handed over in.

parts.note: anagram fodder, nine letters; the apostrophe counts for nothing

explanation.surface: A consignment of fruit belonging to some importers.
explanation.walkthrough: The apostrophe is load-bearing: 'importers' bananas' reads as a possessive, which hides the fact that the second word is an instruction about the first.
explanation.definitionFit: To misreport something is to describe it wrongly: 'mis-' does the work of 'inaccurately' and 'report' the work of 'describe'.

clue.text: Regressive 'topless' wordplay, not entirely new: Everyman prompting weariness

indicators.note: To regress is to go back the way you came, so the letters gathered so far get written out in the opposite direction.
The top of a word is the letter it starts with, and a topless one has lost it; the quotation marks are the setter owning up to the pun.
Not entirely means all of it bar the end, so the final letter of the word is left off.

parts.note: wordplay is a pun, and the pun is beheaded here to leave two letters
the word gives up its final letter
the compiler's own name in the clue stands for the compiler, who is 'I'

explanation.surface: Everyman apologising for a stale, backward-looking pun.
explanation.walkthrough: The reversal covers only the two trimmed words; the last piece is added after it, which is why the whole thing does not simply read backwards.
explanation.definitionFit: Ennui is the listless boredom of having nothing worth doing — a weariness of the spirit rather than of the legs.

clue.text: What remains of razed supermarket, you say: a few small hairs

indicators.note: Saying a thing rather than writing it leaves only its sound, and this sound turns out to be spelt a completely different way.

parts.note: burn a supermarket down and what is left of its long shelved gangways is aisle ashes — and that phrase is the one being said aloud

explanation.surface: A burnt-out supermarket, and whatever the fire left behind.
explanation.walkthrough: The place where the two words divide moves when you say them: the l of 'aisle' slides across the gap into the second word. 'Razed' is the only word telling you a fire has happened at all.
explanation.definitionFit: Eyelashes are the short hairs fringing the eyelid, so 'a few small hairs' describes them plainly, if from a long way round.

clue.text: C17-18 satirist who penned Shake It Off

definitions.meaning: the Dublin author of Gulliver's Travels and A Modest Proposal
the American singer whose 2014 single that was

explanation.surface: A satirist dead for three centuries credited with a modern pop hit.
explanation.walkthrough: Two people three hundred years apart share the surname, and the clue runs them into one sentence as though a single writer had done both jobs.
explanation.definitionFit: Jonathan Swift wrote Gulliver's Travels and A Modest Proposal in the 1600s and 1700s; Taylor Swift wrote 'Shake It Off' in 2014.

clue.text: Very rainy — I'm surprised — somewhere in S Africa

parts.note: so tired means very tired
wet weather is rainy weather
the cry of surprise written as a single letter, as in 'O, the shame of it'

explanation.surface: A grumble about the downpour, broken off by an exclamation.
explanation.walkthrough: The dashes make the middle phrase read as an aside, and that is what hides it: the interruption is not commentary but the third piece of the charade.
explanation.definitionFit: Soweto is the vast township on the south-western edge of Johannesburg — its name is short for South Western Townships.

clue.text: Underarm's faltering: beat this!

definitions.note: The definition names the answer by what is done to it rather than by a phrase you could swap for it in a sentence, which is why it arrives as an order.

indicators.note: A faltering step is one that loses its footing, and letters that lose their footing come down in a different order.

parts.note: anagram fodder, nine letters; the apostrophe counts for nothing

explanation.surface: Somebody's deodorant giving up on them, with a challenge thrown down.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Beat this!' reads as a boast on the surface and as a pointer in the parse — the thing beaten is the answer — while the apostrophe quietly supplies the S the fodder needs.
explanation.definitionFit: A snare drum is the sharp, rattling drum in a kit, played with sticks — 'beat this' points at it by the action it exists for.

clue.text: Ex-president, leader of Zimbabwe okays reforms adopting rand

indicators.note: To reform something is to form it again in another shape, which is what these letters do.
Adopting somebody is taking them into the household, so the letters already gathered open up and the last piece goes inside.
The leader of a word is the letter at its head, so only the country's initial is taken.

parts.note: the letter the country's name begins with
anagram fodder, five letters
R is the rand, South Africa's currency

explanation.surface: An African leader signing off reforms paid for in rand.
explanation.walkthrough: Everything on the surface is southern African — a leader, reforms, the rand — and the answer is French, which is the distance the clue is trading on.
explanation.definitionFit: Nicolas Sarkozy was President of France from 2007 to 2012, so 'ex-president' names him by the office he no longer holds.

clue.text: American made American biopic

parts.note: a = American, the standard one-letter abbreviation
taken at face value, four letters as written
the US is the same word abbreviated the other standard way

explanation.surface: An American-produced film about an American subject.
explanation.walkthrough: One word appears twice and shortens two different ways, one letter the first time and two the second. The film itself is about a Viennese composer and has no American in it.
explanation.definitionFit: Amadeus is the 1984 film of Mozart's life as told by his jealous rival Salieri, so 'biopic' defines it by genre.

clue.text: American backing school for doctors, one wanting decapitation

indicators.note: Backing something means standing behind it to hold it up, so the American piece goes behind the school rather than in front of it.

parts.note: med school is where doctors are trained
the initials the country is known by

explanation.surface: An American funding a medical school, and someone facing the axe.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Backing' looks like an instruction to turn a piece round and means support instead: it goes behind, not backwards. The last phrase is the definition, naming a figure of Greek myth by the way her story ends.
explanation.definitionFit: Medusa is the snake-haired Gorgon of Greek myth whose head Perseus cut off — killing her meant decapitating her.

clue.text: Party to unwind, so Rolfing a kind of knot

indicators.note: To be party to something is to be within it as one of its parts — a loose instruction, but the sense wanted is being inside the words that follow.

parts.note: seven letters in a row, running from inside the first word through the second and into the third

explanation.surface: A relaxed gathering with some deep-tissue massage on offer.
explanation.walkthrough: Rolfing is a deep-tissue massage that works knots out of muscles, so 'knot' reads as part of the scene rather than as the definition it is.
explanation.definitionFit: The Windsor is the broad triangular knot for a tie, named after the Duke of Windsor, who liked the wide look it gave.

clue.text: Channel, one doing some embroidery

definitions.meaning: the drainage sense: the pipe running under the street
the needlework sense: a person who sews

explanation.walkthrough: The two words are spelt identically and said differently — the drain rhymes with 'newer', the needleworker with 'lower' — and nothing in the clue admits that the pronunciation changes.
explanation.definitionFit: A sewer is the underground channel that carries waste water away, and a sewer — this one rhyming with 'lower' — is somebody working a needle.

clue.text: After a party, journalist shamefaced

indicators.note: After says where the piece goes: the journalist follows the party instead of arriving before it.

parts.note: the article is taken as written, one letter
a bash is a party, especially a loud one
ed is the editor, the crossword's usual newspaperman

explanation.surface: A reporter turning up sheepish the morning after a big night.
explanation.walkthrough: 'After' is both the instruction and the word that makes the sentence read as a hangover story, and ED is the crossword's standing journalist — the editor, always those two letters.
explanation.definitionFit: To be abashed is to be embarrassed and lost for words, which is exactly how a shamefaced person looks.

clue.text: Dance, and unsettle sundry squares?

parts.note: a question that throws you is one that unsettles you
sundry items are some items, an unspecified few
a square is one kind, and the question mark marks the example standing in for the class

explanation.surface: Getting the dance floor going and rattling a few unhip onlookers.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Squares' are unhip people on the surface and geometry in the parse, and the question mark is the setter admitting that one example is standing in for all of them.
explanation.definitionFit: To throw some shapes is British slang for dancing, especially the showy moves people pull on a dance floor.

clue.text: Goods cart, just under 1m in length, rejected

indicators.note: To reject a thing is to throw it back, so the measure is written back to front.

parts.note: a yard is 0.914 of a metre, so a little short of one

explanation.surface: A short delivery cart being turned away at the gate.
explanation.walkthrough: The measure is the trap: '1m' reads as a length in metres, and what is wanted is the imperial unit that falls a few centimetres short of one.
explanation.definitionFit: A dray is the low, sideless cart breweries used to deliver barrels behind a heavy horse — a goods cart of one particular kind.

clue.text: Ornamental band showing RIP — LEFT — DEPARTED

indicators.note: Departed means gone, so the letter just identified leaves the word it was sitting in.

parts.note: to rip a canvas is to slash it
l = left, the standard abbreviation

explanation.surface: A headstone inscription, set out in capitals.
explanation.walkthrough: The capitals and the dashes make the three words read as an epitaph — rest in peace, left us, departed — while each of them is doing a separate job in the wordplay.
explanation.definitionFit: A sash is the broad ribbon worn over one shoulder or round the waist, which is an ornamental band and nothing more.
